Shirley Chisholm. From 1924 to 2005, the first Black woman elected to Congress, representing Brooklyn from 1969 to 1983. A teacher, activist, and fiery orator, she challenged both racism and sexism, embodying the intersectional voice of the late-twentieth-century civil rights and women's movements. She was elected to the House of Representatives from New York's twelfth district in 1968, making her the first Black woman in that chamber. In 1972 she ran for the Democratic presidential nomination under the slogan Unbought and Unbossed, making her the first Black candidate in a major-party primary. She was a former schoolteacher and early childhood education advocate who brought populist energy and moral clarity to legislative debates. In 1971 she co-founded the Congressional Black Caucus and fought vocally against the Vietnam War and poverty. She served fourteen years in the House on education and agriculture committees, championing underserved communities and women's rights. In 1970 she authored Unbought and Unbossed, her influential memoir connecting her personal journey to the broader struggle for Black and women's liberation. She bridged civil rights and women's liberation, challenging both movements to address intersectionality. Her contemporary Barbara Jordan was elected to Congress two years later, pioneering alongside her. Adam Clayton Powell Jr. represented Harlem in the same era and pioneered Black legislative power. And though she faced establishment opposition repeatedly, the urban constituency of Brooklyn, New York, elected her again and again.
